segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: We're pleased to welcome Dr Martin Merrywhether of the Antarctic Centre in Christchurch, New Zealand who has come along to talk to us today about the role of the Centre and the Antarctic Treaty.

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: Now my first question is about the choice of location for the centre. Why Christchurch? Was it because of the climate?

segments.speaker: DOCTOR
segments.en: Well actually New Zealand is the second closest country to Antarctica and Christchurch is often used on Antarctic expeditions.

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: Right, so it's because of where we are . . . coupled with our historical role. So tell us - what is the main purpose of the centre?

segments.speaker: DOCTOR
segments.en: Well ... we have two complementary roles. One is as a scientific base for expeditions and research and the other is as an information centre.

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: Tell us something about the role as a scientific base.

segments.speaker: DOCTOR
segments.en: We're able to provide information about what scientists should take with them to the South Pole- for , the centre contains a clothing warehouse where expeditions are supplied with suitable clothing for the extreme conditions.

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: I suppose you need a bit more than your normal winter coat!

segments.speaker: DOCTOR
segments.en: Yes, exactly and then there's also the spechlist library and mapping serv1ces.

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: Right. And which countries are actually located at the centre?

segments.speaker: DOCTOR
segments.en: Well . . . the centre houses research programmes for New Zealand, for The United States as well as for Italy ... there's even a US post office at the American airforce base here.

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: Really? And what does the visitor's centre offer?

segments.speaker: DOCTOR
segments.en: Well, since very few people will ever experience the Antarctic first hand, the visitors' centre aims to recreate the atmosphere of Antarctica. There's a mock camp site where you can see inside an Antarctic tent and imagine yourself sleeping there. And the centre also acts as a showcase for the unique international co-operation which exists in Antarctica today.

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: What is it actually like at the South Pole? I know you've been there on a number of occasions.

segments.speaker: DOCTOR
segments.en: Yes, I have and each time I'm struck by the awesome beauty of the place. It's magnificent but you can really only visit it in the summer months.

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: October to March.

segments.speaker: DOCTOR
segments.en: Yes, because it's completely dark for four months of the year (pause) ... and in addition it has to be the coldest place on earth.

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: Colder than the North Pole? Why's that?

segments.speaker: DOCTOR
segments.en: Well, unlike the North Pole, which is actually a frozen sea, Antarctica is a land mass shaped like a dome, with the result that the winds blow down the slopes at speeds of up to 150 km an hour and that's what makes it so cold. And one other interesting thing is that Antarctica is the driest continent on earth, surprisingly, and so you have to drink large amounts of water when you're there.

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: How old is Antarctica?

segments.speaker: DOCTOR
segments.en: We're pretty sure it was part of a larger land mass but it broke away from the rest of the continent 170 million years ago.

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: How can you be certain of this?

segments.speaker: DOCTOR
segments.en: ... because fossils and rocks have been discovered in Antarctica which are the same as those found in places such as Africa and Australia.

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: Amazing . .. To think that it was once attached to Africa .. .

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: Now let's just have a look at the Antarctic Treaty. How far back does the idea of an international treaty go?

segments.speaker: DOCTOR
segments.en: Well, as far back as the 19th century, when eleven nations organised an international event.

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: When was that exactly?

segments.speaker: DOCTOR
segments.en: In 1870. And it was called the Polar Research Meeting. And then, not long after that, they organised something called the First International Polar Year.

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: And that took place when exactly?

segments.speaker: DOCTOR
segments.en: Over two years from 1882 to 1883. But it wasn't until the 1950s that the idea of an international treaty was proposed. And in 1959 the Treaty was actually signed.

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: What do you see as the main achievements of the treaty?

segments.speaker: DOCTOR
segments.en: Well, firstly it means that the continent is reserved for peaceful use.

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: That's Article I, isn't it?

segments.speaker: DOCTOR
segments.en: Yes ...

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: That's important since the territory belongs to everyone.

segments.speaker: DOCTOR
segments.en: Yes but not as important as Article 5, which prohibits any nuclear explosions or waste disposal.

segments.speaker: INTERVIEWER
segments.en: Which is marvellous. Well, I'm afraid we're going to have to stop there because I'm afraid we've run out of time. Thanks for coming along today and telling us all about the centre and its work.
